newsitem.title: FRANCE: RENAULT UNIONS WALK OUT OVER VILVOORDE.
newsitem.headline: RENAULT UNIONS WALK OUT OVER VILVOORDE.

text.p: Trade union delegates stormed out of French car maker Renault SA's works council on Thursday after management refused to allow a representative of Belgian workers facing a plant closure to address a meeting, union sources said.

Some 300 workers from the assembly plant at Vilvoorde, near Brussels, came to Paris to protest to Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer, who offered to meet a delegation but would not let a Belgian union leader address the French works council.

The announcement of the closure of the recently-modernised plant in Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene's home town, with the loss of 3,100 direct jobs in June, has triggered widespread anger in Belgium and France. Renault has also announced plans to cut more than 2,700 jobs in France this year.

Belgian works council leader Raymond Smeulders refused to meet Schweitzer separately and read the statement he had planned to deliver to a protest rally outside Renault headquarters in Boulogne-Billancourt in the Paris suburbs.

"Mr Schweitzer, the decision to close Vilvoorde is a cowardly, unproductive and uneconomical decision. I can assure you that we will fight till the end if we must," he declared to cheers from the angry crowd.

"We are ready to discuss all possibilities of keeping the production site in Vilvoorde. Until then, we are going to keep our 'war chest', which is worth quite a lot," he said, referring to the stock of new cars which workers occupying the factory have said they have taken hostage.

French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, alarmed by the Belgian backlash, summoned Schweitzer on Wednesday and, without calling into question the industrial decision to close the plant, urged Renault to open immediate talks with the Belgian workforce and authorities on cushioning the human cost.
A Belgian newspaper reported on Thursday that South Korean car maker KIA was considering buying the Vilvoorde plant.

Financial daily De Financieel-Economische Tijd quoted Jong Chung, KIA Motors Europe's managing director, as saying at the Geneva car show that his firm first had to review the books at Renault Industrie Belgique before making a final decision.
He said KIA would be seeking output of 150,000 cars a year, which would mean the plant would run at full capacity. He did not say which model KIA would be making there.

Renault spokesman Patrick Bessy told the paper: "We are happy with any producer, any industrialist coming forward as a candidate for a takeover. It makes no difference who it is as long as there is a takeover."
